title: Find the length of a linked list (traverse and count nodes).
shortTitle: Find the length of a linked list
keyPoints: The traversal-count approach walks from head to null, incrementing a counter per node, giving O(n) time and O(1) space
The maintained-size approach keeps a size field updated on every add and remove, giving O(1) length lookups
Java's java.util.LinkedList uses a maintained size field, so its size() method returns instantly
If you maintain a size field, every mutation path must update it, or the count drifts out of sync
A traversal count can serve as a correctness audit against a maintained size field in production
Both iterative and recursive counting approaches exist, but iterative is preferred to avoid stack overflow on long lists

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk from head to null with a counter, adding one per node; or keep a size field updated on every mutation for instant lookups.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Traversal count** – walk from `head` to `null`, incrementing a counter for each node; O(n) time, O(1) space.
- **Maintained size** – keep an integer `size` field on the list object that increments on `add` and decrements on `remove`; O(1) to read.
- **Trade-off** – traversal count is always accurate but slow; maintained size is fast but requires every mutation path to update the field correctly.
- **Java standard** – `java.util.LinkedList` internally maintains a `size` field so `size()` returns in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to know how many pending loan applications Rajesh currently has in his queue. A clerk can either start at the first slip and count one by one until the chain ends, or the front desk can maintain a tally board that gets incremented every time a new application arrives and decremented every time one is processed. The tally board is faster to read, but someone must remember to update it on every change.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Traversal Count

  head
   │
   ▼
  [LOAN-001] ──> [LOAN-002] ──> [LOAN-003] ──> null
   count=1        count=2        count=3        loop ends
                                                return 3
```

```text
  Maintained Size Field

  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │  LoanLinkedList             │
  │  head ──> [LOAN-001] ──>...│
  │  size = 3                   │
  │                             │
  │  addFirst() → size++        │
  │  removeFirst() → size--     │
  │  getSize() → return size    │
  └─────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the length of a linked list means counting how many nodes it contains. The most straightforward approach is the traversal count: set a counter to zero, walk from head to null, and increment for each node. This is O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is always correct because it physically visits every node.

The faster alternative is to maintain a `size` field on the list object. You increment it every time you add a node and decrement it every time you remove one. Reading the length then becomes O(1), just returning the field. This is exactly how `java.util.LinkedList` reports its size instantly.

The trade-off is discipline. If you maintain a size field, every single code path that adds or removes a node must update that field. If even one path forgets, the count silently drifts out of sync with the actual structure. In a financial system at National Bank of India, that kind of drift is a serious bug. We keep a traversal-based count available in our audit tools so we can periodically verify that the maintained size still matches the real number of pending loan applications.

The choice between the two approaches comes down to how often you need the length versus how many mutation paths exist. If length is rarely needed, the O(n) walk is simpler and avoids bookkeeping bugs. If length is displayed on every screen refresh, maintaining a size field is worth the extra discipline.

Remember one sentence: count by traversal is always correct in O(n), or maintain a size field for O(1) but update it on every mutation.
